To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Borna disease virus infection of Lewis rats results in the development of a delayed-type hypersensitivty reaction which is characterized by the massive expression of MCH class II antigen on microglial and other cells and by the infiltration of the CNS with T helper cells, B cells and macrophage-like cells.
the encephalitic lesion is dominated by macrophages and CD4+ T lymphocytes and that MHC class II antigens are expressed by lymphatic cells, macrophages, and microglia.
the encephalitic Borna disease is a T cell-mediated disease.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the immunohistochemical investigation of the inflammatory process in experimental Borna disease in the Lewis rat.
the immunohistological analysis of experimental Borna encephalitis, which is a model for a virus-induced immunological disease of the central nervous system.
the immunohistochemical investigation of the immune response in the brain of rats with Borna disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

in Borna disease virus-induced encephalitis a complex immunopathological reaction is operative which is dominated by the presence of macrophages and lymphocytes and which is accompanied by a massive expression of MICH class II antigen.
Borna disease virus infection in the rat is associated with a delayed-type hypersensivity response which may contribute to the pathogenesis of the disease.

the Borna disease virus-induced meningoencephaloencephalitis in Lewis rats is characterized by the presence of a delayed-type hypersensivity reaction with the involvement of macrophages, microglial cells, and T helper lymphocytes, which are the major effector cells of this reaction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

Borna disease virus is a neurotropic virus that induces an inflammatory reaction in the central nervous system (CNS) of rats and that this reaction is characterized by a delayed type hypersensitivity response.
the immune response in Borna disease is characterized by a massive influx of T lymphocytes and macrophages and the expression of MHC antigen by cells of the central nervous system.

Borna disease virus is able to induce a virus-specific immune response in the central nervous system of rats which is characterized by a massive infiltration of inflammatory cells and expression of MHC antigen by microglial cells, macrophages and ependymal lining cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the immune system is a major factor in the development of Borna disease.
we were able to show that the immune response in the brain is very complex and involves many different types of immune cells.
the immune system is not only important in the development of the disease, but also plays an important role in the pathogenesis and the progression of the disease.
